# 17-expanse — sources

Back-test entry `17-expanse.yaml`: Expanse, job sizes predicted at submit time on shared GPU clusters (YC Spring 2026,
P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-05-04 and the Launch HN of 2026-06-01 (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era
where one exists; anything later is marked as later and sits under *Status today*).

- [LYC] Launch YC: "Expanse - Unlock wasted GPU capacity", 2026-05-04 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/QCF-expanse-unlock-wasted-gpu-capacity

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

Cluster operators (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Gregory Lindqvist, Nadia Kowalski, Marco Bianchi → [HN] the measured national cluster and "Datacenters run at roughly 30% to 40% effective utilisation": operators who see the waste and would pay at the founder's band.
- Arjun Mehta → [HN] "large scale compute industries as well, such as quant funds": a quant-fund platform lead who owns the compute budget, sees more waste than the founder's high and decides alone (against the tested department head).

The split (4 of 7 operators at the founder's rung or above; 5 of 6 who give a number at 30% waste or more) is the
author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

## Could not be sourced

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

## Revision 24 (keel-cloud spec 215, 2026-11-04)

The rows keel-e2e-eval spec 134's review moved (`specs/215-the-corpus-fits-the-cards/corpus-rewording.md`, Table 1), before -> after (rule):

- Importance: Guessing memory, GPUs and run time before submitting -> Sizing a job to neither fail nor waste GPUs (`imp-own`)
- Importance: Running out of the group's allocation -> Keeping within the group's GPU-hour allocation (`imp-backwards`, `imp-cause`)
- Current solution: Sized from past runs; it ran as planned -> Ran first time, sized about right (`cs-joined`, `cs-measure`)
- Current solution: Padded it a little; it ran, a little idle -> Ran, holding about twice what it used (`cs-joined`, `cs-measure`)
- Current solution: Doubled everything to be safe; much sat idle -> Ran, holding three times what it used (`cs-joined`, `cs-measure`)
- Current solution: Guessed low; it died and was resubmitted -> Failed partway and had to be resubmitted (`cs-joined`, `cs-measure`)
- Current solution: Copied an old script and hoped -> Never ran to the end (`cs-fail`, `cs-measure`)
- Compatibility: The job went through SLURM or Kubernetes as usual -> could run a monitoring agent on the job's node {asked: could your job have run with a monitoring agent on its node} (`cmp-settled`, `cmp-subject`)
- Compatibility: The source code sat on the cluster -> kept the job's source code on the cluster (`cmp-subject`)
- Compatibility: The job's code was written in Python -> wrote the job's code in Python (`cmp-subject`)
- Relative advantage: The job runs first time, no resubmits -> A job that runs to the end first time (`ra-one`)
- Purchase friction: Letting it read job scripts and source code -> *(dropped)* -- folded into *A security review of an agent on every node* (it is a part of that review); `items` 3 -> 2, the pick (0) unmoved (`pf-overlap`, `pf-object`)
- Purchase friction: A budget line for the department's pilot -> A budget line in the department's plan (`pf-offer`)

screens.why1: Right after I've said how Expanse fits into the way they submit today, asking what it does better than that way is the obvious next step in my solution.

screens.why3: I know exactly what my researchers gain over padding and guessing: jobs that don't die mid-run and smaller requests that clear the queue sooner.
screens.why4: The box takes my two benefits as separate lines, and the single escape chip, 'Leave this out of the study', fits a founder who isn't sure.
screens.why5: Nothing is reworded on this screen; my two benefits stand as I typed them, and the founder-only screen leaks nothing to strangers.
screens.why7: The box asks for 1 to 4 equal benefits, each under nine words, compared with today's way, with the founder's escape; my two rows are distinct, each names one gain, and the one I lead with is a row.

screens.why1: Right after I said what Expanse does better than padding, it is obvious why Keel shows the benefits back for me to check before they are tested.
screens.why2: "Runs to the end first time" and "a shorter wait in the queue" are how anyone submitting to SLURM talks; nothing here would make me read it twice.
screens.why3: Both are things a researcher sees on every submission: whether the job died partway and how long it sat pending.
screens.why4: Two distinct rows, one about the job finishing and one about queue time, no overlap, in my words, and within the 1 to 4 limit.
screens.why5: My "debug failures in seconds, not days" and the smaller request fitting sooner are kept as the two gains I would lead with, and the intro says strangers never see the list.
screens.why7: Every rule on shape and balance is met: two rows, the lead first, both joined with "and", and the fixed four plus "I can't tell" behind it; one rule is bent: the belief's occasion is any last job submission rather than the hard case, a job that failed partway or sat padded, and "runs to the end first time" is something padding already delivers yet is not flagged for me to keep or drop.
screens.instead: Keep both rows; test: For most, with it, their last job that failed partway or sat holding twice what it used would have given them a job that runs to the end first time and a shorter wait in the queue.

screens.why4: The only option is the escape chip, 'Leave this out of the study', which fits a founder who has nothing to test here, and the box takes my rows as typed.

screens.why7: Both rows meet the card: each is one effort of at most 9 words, a base-form verb phrase, a step the researcher takes themselves rather than the operator's install or a security sign-off, with neither repeating Compatibility or Purchase friction; there are 2 rows within 1 to 4, and the founder's escape is present.

screens.why1: Right after I checked the efforts I typed, picking which one strangers get asked about is the obvious next step.

screens.why3: Which effort my researchers would balk at is something I know from the thread and the clusters I have seen.

screens.why1: Right before strangers see the study, it is obvious to decide whether to collect emails from people who want to try it, and as a founder onboarding paid pilots I want those leads.

screens.why3: Whether I want sign-ups is my own call and I know the answer at once: yes, we are actively onboarding pilots.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right under the title with '4 counted' beside it, and every card adds '5 needed to call it', so I know the answer and the number behind it, though the header oddly names only Compatibility when all three cards fall short the same way.

screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do: not that one more counted researcher would settle each card, not whom to send it to, not whether to change the study.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing; n=7 and 4 counted are visible everywhere, and the low count is said outright as 'too few to call'.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', so I know why there's no call: one more counted answer.
screens.why_b2: The bars are plain (2 yes, 2 conditional, 0 against), but the strip's 'your bar · 4 of 5' with a ghost cell made me stop: is that 4 for out of 5 answered, or 4 counted out of the 5 needed, and what does a 1-in-3-against bar have to do with a marker at 4?

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' is stated with '4 counted · 5 needed to call it' right beside it, but the screen never says how the 4 split (only '1 against'), so I cannot see which way the line leans.

screens.why1: As the opening screener it plainly checks I work at the scale the study is about, and I can see why it comes first.
screens.why2: Clusters, jobs and GPUs are my everyday words, so I can answer this on the first reading.
screens.why3: I know roughly how big the clusters I submit to are, so I can answer from my own work without guessing.
screens.why4: For a gate, Yes and No are complete and distinct, and the dimension rules forbid an escape here, so its absence is correct.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's 100-plus-GPU segment and says nothing about any product or plan.
screens.why6: It is short and is one question with two options, though the template's 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.' sounds a bit stiff next to just 'Yes or no.'

screens.why1: Right after the 100-GPU screener, asking whether one of my jobs got killed this week is the obvious next thing for a study about guessing memory, GPUs and wall time.
screens.why2: Job killed before it finished is exactly how I'd say it about an OOM kill or hitting the time limit on SLURM, so I get it on first read.
screens.why3: I know straight away whether any of my runs got killed in the last five working days; I watch the squeue and sacct output and the error logs.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it and both are true of someone; the chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to this gate.
screens.why5: It asks the costly thing that goes wrong, a job killed mid-run, with no product, plan or founder's term leaking to me.
screens.why6: One short sentence followed by Yes or no is easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: The gate asks the problem rather than the routine of submitting jobs, so a researcher whose runs all finished truly says No and one who got killed says Yes, with two fixed answers in order and no escape, as the card requires.

screens.why1: Part 2 opens on the idea, and this card sits right after the screens on clusters and killed jobs, so it is obvious why I am shown it here.
screens.why2: SLURM, Kubernetes, node, walltime, submission script and GPU memory are my everyday words, though 'GPU memory, memory, CPUs' reads a little clumsy.
screens.why3: Guessing memory and walltime before I submit, and losing a run when I under-request, is exactly what I do every week.
screens.why4: A card to read; there are no options.
screens.why5: It reads as the founder's own pitch shown on purpose, using my words for my work and none of the founder's internal terms for people like me.
screens.why6: Said aloud, the middle line is a mouthful: two back-to-back lists ('source code, submission script and hardware', then 'GPU memory, memory, CPUs and walltime') plus three more features, so it is hard to hold in one hearing.
screens.instead: Imagine Expanse, a tool on your cluster that predicts what each job needs. When you submit, it reads your code and script and predicts GPU memory, CPUs and walltime, warns you before a job would fail, and tells you why one did. The people building it believe it would be of use on every job you submit.

screens.why1: A question about how my job gets to the cluster is plausible right after the idea card, but jumping from a tool that predicts resource needs to where my source code lives is abrupt, because the card never says the tool needs my code.
screens.why2: Source code, cluster and job submission are my everyday words, so I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I know where my training code sat when I last submitted, whether on the shared filesystem, in a container image or pulled from git.
screens.why4: Yes, with some steps is odd for a fact about where code was kept, since it was either on the cluster or not, and a container image or git clone at launch sits awkwardly between the options.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's own terms leaks beyond the idea card shown on purpose.
screens.why6: It is short, one question and three short options I can hold, with one escape said last.
screens.why7: Running on a shared SLURM or Kubernetes cluster almost always means the code is on the cluster's filesystem or image, so nearly everyone answers Yes and nothing can count against the belief, while the step the pitch rests on (trusting a predicted memory, GPU and time request instead of padding to the max) goes untested.
screens.instead: On your last job submission, could you have used a predicted memory and run time instead of your own padded guess? Yes, easily; Yes, most of the time; Only sometimes; No; I can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after the Expanse card, asking whether it would have beaten what I did last time is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: "Done that better" has nothing to point at, because the question never says the 'that' is guessing memory, GPUs and wall time before I sbatch, so I have to re-read to work out what 'that' is.
screens.why3: I submitted jobs this week and I know exactly how I sized them, so I can judge whether a predictor would have helped.
screens.why4: The four answers plus I can't tell cover everything I'd say, they don't overlap, and they're words I'd use.
screens.why5: The circumstance lost its point, guessing the resources before submitting, and 'a tool' drops what the card said Expanse is, so the founder's meaning drifted a little.
screens.why6: It's short, one question, four options I can hold, and one escape said last.
screens.why7: The four fixed answers and the escape are right, but the occasion is any submission rather than the hard case where the guess mattered, and 'that' leaves unclear which better is meant, so one rule is bent.
screens.instead: Think of the last time you had to guess memory, GPUs and run time for a job. Would Expanse, a tool that predicts each job's needs, have done that better for you, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: After the idea card and the 'would it do better' question, asking whether I'd actually trust its sizes instead of padding is the obvious next thing to ask me.
screens.why2: 'Padding your requests' is exactly how I'd say it, but the second option reads backwards, so I had to stop and re-read it.
screens.why3: I pad every submission because under-requesting gets my run killed, so I know exactly whether I'd drop that habit.
screens.why4: 'Only if they risk my job failing' is inverted nonsense; the true conditional answer, 'only if they don't risk my job getting killed', is missing.
screens.why5: The step is the idea card's own, the suggested sizes in place of my padding, and nothing beyond that leaks to me.
screens.why6: It's short and the list holds, but 'only if they risk your job failing' is a mouthful that sounds wrong out loud, and I'd stall on it.
screens.why7: The step is mine to take, on the one measure, with 2 for and 2 against and the escape apart, but the conditional rung's own condition is inverted, so that rung can't be answered as meant and only plain Yes really carries the 'for' side.
screens.instead: To use Expanse, you'd use its suggested sizes instead of padding your requests. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Only if it didn't get my jobs killed · Probably not · No · I can't tell
